newsitem.title: USA: Clinton budget plan foresees balance by 2002.
newsitem.headline: Clinton budget plan foresees balance by 2002.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday unveiled a $1.69 trillion budget proposal cutting $98.4 billion in taxes over five years yet still reaching balance by 2002.

The fiscal 1998 budget, which was formally released on Thursday after being widely leaked on Wednesday, offers a range of tax cuts designed to benefit families, encourage higher education and ease the taxation of most home sales.

Covering the year beginning Oct. 1, the budget would in part offset these by closing corporate tax loopholes and by restoring expired excise and other taxes that, taken together, would raise $76 billion over the five years.
It forecast that the 1998 deficit would narrow to $120.6 billion from 1997's $125.6 billion and gradually shrink over the next three years to become a $17 billion surplus in 2002.
In putting forward the proposal, Clinton, a Democrat, was essentially presenting his opening offer in the annual budget talks between the president and the Republican-held Congress.
In doing so, he is returning to the primary battleground between the two parties since the Republicans won majority control of the Senate and House of Representatives in 1994.
In a message accompanying the budget, Clinton noted the budget deficit has been cut by more than 60 percent since he took office in 1993 and said he wanted to finish the job.

"Over the last four years, my administration and Congress have already done much of the hard work of reaching balance in 2002," Clinton said. "I want to work with Congress to achieve the final increment of deficit cutting and bring the budget into balance for the first time since 1969."
But the initial reaction to the president's budget from Representative John Kasich, the influential Ohio Republican who chairs the House Budget Committee, did not appear enthusiastic.
"The president of the United States, while declaring the era of big government at an end, every day comes up with another programme to actually expand government," he told CNN.
The White House said it expected some criticism but felt the Republicans were taking their budget proposal seriously.

"We certainly expect criticism," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry. "But the most encouraging thing to the president is that this budget is being received seriously and it clearly will be the basis of further discussions ... It is not being cast aside as a document dead on arrival."

The key differences between the two parties over the past two years have been over how much to cut taxes and how much to reduce spending, particularly on popular "entitlements" like the Medicare health care programme for the elderly.

Clinton's proposed $98.4 billion in tax cuts included a $500 per child credit, a $1,500 tax credit or $10,000 tax deduction for college tuition, and an extension of the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales to $500,000 per couple.

At the same time, the budget proposed raising $34.3 billion by closing corporate tax loopholes and extending expiring excise and other taxes worth $41.7 billion, leading to such tax revenue increases of $76 billion over five years.
It would also raise $36.1 billion from sales of broadcast spectrum licenses to private industry over the five years.
As previously reported, the budget would trim $100 billion over five years from projected spending on the politically sensitive Medicare health care programme for the elderly.

Burson-Marsteller analyst Stan Collender said he found the budget credible in its economic assumptions, but less so in its planned spending cuts of about $80 billion from defence and $58 billion from non-defence discretionary programmes.
"The credibility gets strained a little bit in the out years on discretionary spending," Collender said. "The cuts are going to be difficult."
